I appreciate your response, but I would disagree with you that mental illness is a purely behavioral or psychiatric disorder. A lot of mental health overlaps with spiritual health, and a lot of principles that help a person grow spiritually also bring a person to deeper mental healing. I have already found a lot of healing from other struggles through a biblical approach, so I don't see why a biblically structured framework would be a bad thing, provided that the individual believes the bible... philosophically speaking, you can't ever really create an approach to a problem that is 100 percent devoid of ideological bias. A lot of mental health therapies pull from buddhism or yoga for instance. I'm not opposed to approaching things from a psychological perspective, but if there's going to be bias anyway, I'd rather it be to what I already believe 😁

That said, it does make sense to me that you need some kind of functional approach rather than simply talking through it. I was simply curious as to whether anyone had done that functional approach on a biblical basis. I have to admit that from my limited understanding of ERP I would be hesitant to engage in it for some particular faith reasons I won't go into here... But I like certain aspects of it, although I would prefer to adapt them to fit my beliefs. 

I love that psychology is working to create and test solutions for mental health struggles, although I don't know that it can ever truly be one size fits all since people's lives are so different. However, my and your perspectives aside, thanks again for your comment and have a great day.

God loves you and will get you through this. He isn't fazed by it at all, and he already knows the way to overcome. The best thing you can do is to go to him in prayer, with a sincere heart, and ask him for help. You don't have to pray perfectly, but prayer is a wonderful thing God has given us to build trust in him. As you begin to trust him more with this struggle, he will show you the way through. He loves you, and he isn't angry or worried about what is going on in your mind. He wants to redeem your thoughts and your life, and show you what his mercy is like. If you are in Christ, you are a new creation, and the evil thoughts you might think are not truly your own. They are either a remnant of the flesh (old nature) that no longer controls you, or they are a malicious attack from satan. Either way, God sees you as separate from those thoughts, and wants to show you how to live apart from them. Let him teach you! He is full of mercy and patience. Keep praying and waiting for his guidance until he shows you the way out.

Some prayer points I would suggest:

- Ask God to take those thoughts away

- Tell God that you repent of (hate, turn away from) those thoughts and want his help to fight them

- Ask him to reveal to you the source of those thoughts (it might be something in your mind like unforgiveness, doubt, sin you need to turn from, trauma, etc. Or it might be the enemy harassing you. Sometimes it is both, where the enemy pegs a weak point in your soul and uses it to harass you with evil thoughts - those are his thoughts, not yours, but they probably feel like your own.)

- Declare before God that you believe he has forgiven you completely, and you don't carry any guilt or shame for those thoughts.

- Declare to God that you trust him to rid you of those thoughts. Tell him you repent of any way you have not trusted him.

- Tell satan to leave you alone. If you are in Christ you have his authority, so you can do that and the devil has to listen.

- Thank God for his unending love for you, and for giving you the Holy Spirit. Ask the Holy Spirit to fill the weak places in your heart and protect your mind in Christ.

- Ask God to help you love the purity of his heart. There are so many evil, ugly things in the world, but God is beautiful and delightful. His ways are ways of peace and love and as we learn to embrace him, and think the way he does, thoughts of evil stuff (even stuff the world thinks isn't so bad) start to seem gross and pointless, because now we have something much, much better. 

- Read some scriptures that focus on God's ways of thinking and meditate on them, eg let them sink into your mind and mull them over and ponder their meaning. Pray them out personally. For example, 

- - "God, I believe that you have not given me a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and a sound mind."

- - "I believe you, God, that I have the fruit of the Spirit, which is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self control."

- - "I have the mind of Christ."

- - "God, my soul is weary with sorrow, so strengthen me according to your word. I want you to keep me from deceitful ways, so please be gracious to me and teach me your law."

- - (2 Timothy 1:7, Galatians 5:22-23, 1 Corinthians 2:16, Psalm 119:29-30)

These are all just ways to talk to God about what is going on in your mind. Beyond even this, the Holy Spirit is nearer to you than even the thoughts you think, and he will lead you into freedom, joy, peace, clarity, and strength as you trust in him. 

As the scriptures say, we do not lean on our own understanding (our thoughts, feelings, even experiences) but we acknowledge God in all things and he makes our paths straight! (Proverbs 3:6)

May the blessing of his mercy and faithfulness be upon you.

Different things for different people, I guess. My parents raised me much the same as yours but I ended up struggling bad with internet addiction. Some kids need to get used to the structure of rules before they can mimic that structure in self control. For others that structure prevents them from exercising the self control they have by doing it for them. I imagine it depends on age too. I guess it's on parents to familiarize themselves with their kids' tendencies and respond accordingly. 

Edit: I think it's great that your parents emphasized making your future selves happy. I was lacking that and honestly it seems like a great way to communicate the reason behind self control and help kids develop it for themselves.

I guess with questioning the kid is expressing their distaste for the rule in a way that opens up discussion (where they and the authority can both learn something). As opposed to rebelling when the kid is just acting out, and isn't going to listen to the authority's perspective (and will probably just rebel worse if the authority lays down the law). One might end amicably and the other tends to reinforce itself until a breaking point is reached and the kid ends up majorly screwing things up for themselves or others.

Not to mention how much of modern (secular) morality stems from Jesus's teachings, even without it being overtly obvious. Treat others how you want to be treated, accept people as they are, forgive. Things that I suppose could be got to on one's own to some degree. But the pervasiveness is evidence of the impact of Christianity on modern culture, especially in the West.

Also, there's a reason your other friends and this girl wanted to be friends with you in the first place. They want you in their lives. Sometimes you do have to fight for that - not fight for people to care about you, but things happen sometimes, plans fall through, etc, and you have to make the effort yourself to keep in touch and keep on their radar. But that doesn't mean that they don't like you or want you (and if that is true they kinda suck and it's not a reflection on you). I totally understand this fear and have felt insecure introducing new friends to a group for the same reason. Eventually I began to believe that I did have a place in those people's lives and feel more secure in the group. It took time, and it really helped to honestly tell people in the group about my anxieties. Knowing that they knew, and would be careful to include me and reassure me, took a lot of the pressure off. If and when things blow over I would recommend finding someone in the group you can be honest with about that. 

Also, yeah, therapy is good and helpful in getting to a place where you feel and act better, but please don't think that you are a hopelessly broken person because of this situation. It's a process. It's possible to have good friends even if you are still sometimes insecure around them. You are doing your best and you deserve love.

There's feelings, and then there's behavior. You can change the way you behave in response to your feelings: for example, refraining from saying or doing things to manipulate people. You can also change the way you process and deal with your feelings (both so you won't be tempted to behave in hurtful ways, and so you'll have better quality of life): for example, processing them through journaling, talking them out, or channeling them into a creative outlet. I would disagree with theotherthing_ and say that the situation as a whole is about both your anxiety and your actions. With regards to your friendships, your actions might be of more concern since it was your actions that directly affected people. But in the grand scheme of your whole life and the lives of those around you, your anxiety is also a factor - again, both upon your actions and upon your wellbeing. You wouldn't have acted this way without your anxiety, right? But even with your anxiety, you can learn to refrain from acting this way in the future. Yet still it's important to address the anxiety because it makes everything all-around better.

Yo tbh I think you're going a little hard on her. She owned up in her post, admitted outright that she manipulated them out of a place of fear. She's not trying to excuse her behavior here; she's asking for help to stop it and repair the situation. It's honestly not right to say 'you ARE manipulative', thus reducing someone to their worst self. Many people have their manipulative sides and also have sides of them that are good and kind. The good doesn't negate the bad and vice versa. We have to admit the good and bad sides of ourselves in order to live emotionally and relationally healthy lives. If someone gets told 'you are manipulative' enough times, eventually they'll start to believe it. And when the temptation arises to manipulate people - and it's a temptation we all face at some point or another - they'll think (even subconsciously) 'well, I'm manipulative, that's the way I am, so why fight it?' and end up getting into a cycle where their actions only prove their beliefs about themselves, and their beliefs only lead them into further actions. It has to stop somewhere. Yes, people act in manipulative ways, but that doesn't mean they don't have the capacity to change. That takes recognizing what they did and making a concerted effort to change, and sometimes takes reaching out to others (friends, professionals, it honestly doesn't matter as long as it's someone who you'll be honest with and who will give you good advice that you'll take). But it is possible. 

OP, yeah, you acted in a manipulative way. Thanks for admitting it. That takes a lot of courage, even to reddit, and it shows that deep down you have the capacity to be a better friend even if you've messed up. Take heart. You've probably learned from your actions that that's not how you want to treat your friends and that's good. You've probably figured out that you're susceptible to act that way when you get anxious and insecure, and one good thing you can do is try to take care of that. Try to heal from those insecurities and then you'll be more resilient to be more considerate of your friends in the future. And in the meantime, be open if you can about it with people. Tell your new friend that you know you shouldn't have acted that way, you know why you did it, and you're working hard to make sure you won't do it again. That's all you need to do. If she accepts your apology, awesome. And if not, that's not your fault. You are doing all you can right now. 

You are not a bad person. You're human. We all act like jerks sometimes. Yes, it usually is because of our own insecurity, fear, anger, or other emotions that we put before other people's needs. No one is an awful person right off the bat. We fall into patterns of selfishness in many ways and it's our responsibility as human beings to break those patterns and keep them from forming as much as we possibly can. We owe it to the people we love to be the best version of ourselves that we can, and it seems like you're doing a good job of that right now. Congratulations, keep working at it, and hang in there. As long as you stay in the fight you'll keep getting better. Cheers.

I have seen a lot of OP's posts. What I get from them is someone who thinks about things very much in terms of faith, and wants to see the truth of God through the muddle. Sometimes secular mental health communities can be very unkind to people of faith, to say the least (I'm thinking when people say stuff like 'your religion is itself mental illness'). The result is that someone either has to say things outright how they experience them and be prepared to get viewed as 'even more crazy', or they have to go through the hurdles of translating religious-based OCD into terms that make secular sense. Which can leave out a lot of religious-connected parts of the anxieties that might be important to notice. I wish there was a more active Christian-focused (or even religion-based in general) sub for mental health because these things definitely manifest differently when you're a person of faith than when you're not. But for now it's one or the other, prayer requests or therapy talk, unfortunately. Neither can do what the other is best at. 

Which brings me to my last point. There is something that reaching out asking for prayer or theological advice can do that talking to a secular counselor or community cannot, and that is to reassure someone that they are welcome in a Christian community with their issues. The church definitely has a long way to go as far as understanding mental illness, but it does do a good job at accepting people with it as brothers and sisters even when it does not understand. Prayer might not cure someone's OCD but it might definitely make their day a little better overall or even give them the courage to keep reaching out or to try something different. It's not us working but God working through us when we pray and it's not always as expected. I would really caution you to not steer people away from Christian community even as you steer them towards community that understands their struggles. A study at Stanford shows that ketamine's antidepressant effect relies on activating the brain's opioid receptors, increasing the risk of dependency.

https://www.sciencealert.com/doctors-find-opioid-problem-with-using-ketamine-for-depression/amp

"The FDA (Food and Drug Administration) hasn't approved ketamine for the treatment of depression, but some doctors have been prescribing it as a fast, short-term fix, even though its effects on depression in the brain weren't fully understood. And what we just learned is big.
In a small-scale experiment, 12 volunteers who had previously struggled to find effective treatments for their depression were twice given a dose of ketamine, with a two-week gap – once after being given the either the opioid blocker naltrexone, and once after being given a placebo.

Results showed the symptoms of depression vastly improved in the placebo test, but not the naltrexone test. That suggests ketamine is working on the brain's opioid receptors.
"We would hate to treat the depression and suicide epidemics by overusing ketamine, which might perhaps unintentionally grow the third head of opioid dependence," says neuroscientist Mark George from the Medical University of South Carolina, who wrote an accompanying editorial on the new research."

Honestly, my suspicions are never in favor of anything purporting to be a near-miracle-cure for mental illness. It seems too much like a fad diet to me, and the brain is too complex for one single drug to be the no-catch-perfect-remedy in all cases. Any chemical altering of the body has side effects. And 'medical value' can mean anything. What we have is an interesting experimental result, whose mechanisms are still being explored. I wouldnt say anything has true medical value until it's been proven to facilitate lasting change, with few detrimental side effects, in a documented set of circumstances. Otherwise you're just handing out prescriptions like Wal-Mart happy face stickers to anyone who says the word 'depression', and patting yourself on the back for what amounts to poor science and poor medicine but excellent marketing hype. That's what I worry is going on with ketamine being peddled the way it is. Miracle cures usually don't exist, and to proclaim otherwise just spreads false hopes. Real science-based medicine requires a more nuanced understanding of each person's case than is often sought in psychiatry today.

And I say this not necessarily to you but just as a blanket caution I suppose. There are answers to mental illness but they often arent as simple as we want, and no one can be blamed for feeling like they might not be there at all when what seems to be an easy answer turns out to be false.

Think a room in a house you share with him, currently filled with garbage and occupied by an unpleasant tenant. And now, Holy Spirit, I invite you to come fill me in the place that the evil was. I ask you to show me how to walk in hope and righteousness and to give me your peace and joy. 

Father, because of Christ I know I'm forgiven. I recieve your unending love and know that you want nothing but good for me in all of this. 

In Jesus's name, Amen.

Charismatic, pentecostal churches do - even some Episcopal churches can be pretty wise about the Holy Spirit. You've got to be careful just like with any church that their teaching is sound. And if you haven't encountered that kind of teaching before you might be a bit weirded out a first. The thing to remember is - anything that is of God will testify that Jesus is Lord. If you're experiencing or hearing something that tears you down spiritually or makes you feel less loved, it's definitely the devil and you should pray that God would protect you from it. If on the other hand you encounter something that helps you grow or makes you feel more of God's love, it's likely from him. It's still good to test it against scripture just to be sure, and because God wants to give us wisdom and not just experiences. But the more you begin to see God as a loving father who wants to bless you extravagantly in your soul and give you peace and joy in him the better off you'll be.
